title: Concatenated Dictionary Words
statement: You are given a list `words` of distinct, non-empty, lowercase words. A word is a "compound" if it can be written as the concatenation of two or more words that also appear in `words` (each part must be strictly shorter than the compound, and a word may never use itself as a part). The same list word may be reused as different parts of one compound. Return the list of all compound words. The result must be sorted in lexicographic (dictionary) order. Return an empty list if no word qualifies. For example, with words `["cat", "cats", "dog", "catsdogcats"]`, `catsdogcats` is a compound because it splits as `cats + dog + cats`, reusing the word `cats`.
hints: Every part of a compound is itself in the list, so you are repeatedly asking 'is this prefix a known word?' — what structure answers prefix/word queries in one downward walk?

Insert all words into a trie, then segment each candidate with a DFS: the invariant is that whenever you reach an is_word node mid-string you have TWO live options — cut and jump back to the root for the next part, or keep descending the current branch — and you must explore both.

For candidate w, run dfs(pos, pieces): descend from the root over w[pos:]; at any node with is_word, if pos hit the end return pieces>=1 (at least two parts total), otherwise recurse dfs(next_index, pieces+1) and also continue deeper; committing to the shortest matching prefix (e.g. 'cat' before 'cats') is the classic bug this two-branch search avoids.
